\hypersetup{pdftitle={Every independent apex of an even cycle is common: Lean blueprint},pdfauthor={Mathematical expansion and exact certificate audit},pdfsubject={Complete proof and formalization blueprint; not an implemented Lean proof}}

\title{Every independent apex of an even cycle is common\\[5pt]
\large A certificate-complete mathematical blueprint for Lean}
\author{Detailed expansion and audit of the supplied universal proof}
\date{September 26, 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\noindent\textbf{Status.}
This is a complete conventional proof, with its exact finite certificates, of commonality of
$C_n^{+k}$ for every even $n\ge4$ and every integer $k\ge1$.  The stronger relative inequality
is proved for $k\ge3$.  The four collections of certificate matrices are unchanged from
\emph{Every independent apex of an even cycle is common} \cite{universal}; both the original
checks and a separately implemented exact arithmetic audit have been rerun.  The present
organization adds a finite-matrix and dyadic-approximation route so that a formalization
need not construct infinite-dimensional operator traces.  Every named declaration below is
a proposed Lean declaration, not a claim that Lean has checked it.  No Lean compiler was
run in preparing this blueprint.

\paragraph{Scope of the word ``proof''.}
The mathematical inequalities are proved below, with the four large identities proved by
finite rational data and a general soundness argument.  For a Lean development, the
certificate equalities, positive factorizations, and soundness argument must all become
kernel-checked theorems.  A Python success message is not substituted for any such theorem.
The source contains the complete rational matrices and replay programs; there is no
unspecified optimization problem, parameter region, or asymptotic remainder.

\clearpage
\tableofcontents
\clearpage

\section{Target, conventions, and proof organization}
\label{sec:target}

The consolidated short-cycle manuscript is called \emph{the note} \cite{note}.  The preceding
unrestricted manuscript is called \sourceuniversal\ \cite{universal}.  The core inequalities,
the three-apex weights, and the four certificates below are those of \sourceuniversal.
The finite-dimensional reduction and the expanded equality argument are additions made
here for formalization.  Neither the earlier cycle-specific covering trees nor the eventual
cutoff is an input.

\begin{definition}[Kernels, densities, and independent apices]
\label{def:densities}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.homDensity}
Let $(\Omega,\lambda)$ be a probability space.  A bounded symmetric kernel is a measurable
$L:\Omega^2\to\R$ with $L(x,y)=L(y,x)$ and a specified finite bound for $|L|$.
For a finite simple graph $F=(V,E)$, define
\[
 t(F,L)=\int_{\Omega^V}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E}L(x_i,x_j)\,d\lambda^V(\mathbf x).
\]
Each unordered edge is used once.  A graphon has values in $[0,1]$.  Set
\[
 M(F,W)=t(F,W)+t(F,1-W).
\]
The graph $F^{+k}$ has vertex set $V\sqcup\Fin(k)$ and edge set consisting of the old edges
and all pairs with one old and one new vertex.  It has no edges between new vertices.
For $n\ge3$, $C_n$ has vertices $\Fin(n)$ and edges $\{i,i+1\pmod n\}$.
For $j\ge0$, $P_j$ denotes the path with $j$ edges on $\Fin(j+1)$.  The symbols
$K_{u,v}$ and $K_{u,v,w}$ denote complete multipartite graphs with the indicated part sizes.
\end{definition}

All integrals are ordinary real integrals.  They exist because a finite product of bounded
measurable functions on a probability space is integrable.  For graphons on $[0,1]$, a.e.
bounds and symmetry are sufficient: Lemma~\ref{lem:representative} supplies a pointwise
representative.  On a finite space every tuple, including tuples with repeated host values,
is included.  The densities are homomorphism densities, not injective densities.

\begin{lemma}[Vertex and edge counts]
\label{lem:counts}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.apexCycle_edgeCount}
\uses{def:densities}
\proved For $n\ge4$,
\[
 |V(C_n^{+k})|=n+k,\qquad |E(C_n^{+k})|=n(k+1).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The two vertex sets are disjoint.  The $n$ cycle edges are distinct: equality of two unordered
successor pairs either gives the same starting vertex or reverses two successors, and the
latter would imply $n\mid2$, impossible for $n\ge4$.  Each of the $nk$ cross pairs is a
different new edge.  Old edges and cross pairs belong to disjoint edge sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Normalization and signed kernel]
\label{def:normalization}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.normalizedApexDensity}
\uses{def:densities,lem:counts}
Put $U=2W-1$ and $S_\sigma=1+\sigma U$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$.  The sign always has
probability $1/2$.  For even $n\ge4$, use the note's normalization
\[
 A_{n/2,k}=2^{n(k+1)-1}M(C_n^{+k},W),\qquad R_n=2^{n-1}M(C_n,W).
\]
The first subscript of $A$ is half the cycle length.  More generally, for every finite graph,
\[
 \E_\sigma t(F,S_\sigma)=2^{|E(F)|-1}M(F,W).
\]
The expression on the last right side is interpreted as $M(F,W)/2$ when $E(F)$ is empty.
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}
For $\sigma=1$ the kernel is $2W$, and for $\sigma=-1$ it is $2(1-W)$.  Factoring a $2$
from each edge and averaging the two signs proves the identity, including the empty graph.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Universal commonality, relative form, and equality]
\label{thm:main}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.commonality_all_even_all_apices}
\uses{def:normalization}
\proved For every graphon $W$, every even integer $n\ge4$, and every integer $k\ge1$,
\[
 M(C_n^{+k},W)\ge 2^{1-n(k+1)}.
\]
Equality holds if and only if $W=1/2$ almost everywhere.  For every $k\ge3$, one also has
\[
 A_{n/2,k}(W)\ge R_n(W)\ge1.
\]
No relative assertion for all graphons at $k=2$ is part of this theorem.
\end{theorem}

The proof is completed in Theorem~\ref{thm:graphon-main} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:main-equality}.  For Lean, state the principal inequalities in normalized
form first; the power $2^{1-n(k+1)}$ can then be written as
$1/2^{n(k+1)-1}$.  This avoids natural-number subtraction in a negative exponent.

\paragraph{Real powers.}
Whenever an exponent such as $n/4$, $3/2$, or $k/s$ is not a natural number, it is a real
exponent of a nonnegative real number.  In Lean, the intended operation is \code{Real.rpow},
not natural-number division or natural-number exponentiation.  All such exponents in this
proof are strictly positive, except in elementary helper statements where $x^0=1$ is
explicitly permitted.  At $x=0$ and positive exponent, $x^p=0$.

\paragraph{Finite-first organization.}
Sections~\ref{sec:density-algebra}--\ref{sec:finite-completion} prove the needed inequalities
for a symmetric matrix $U$ with entries in $[-1,1]$, on an arbitrary nonempty finite uniform
probability space.  The graph size of this matrix is unrestricted.  Sections~\ref{sec:approx}
and~\ref{sec:equality} pass to every graphon and prove the equality case.  The certificate
soundness lemmas themselves hold on any probability space.  Only finite-dimensional
spectral theory is required by this organization.

\section{Algebra of densities and probability moments}
\label{sec:density-algebra}

\begin{lemma}[Relabelling, isolated vertices, and disjoint unions]
\label{lem:density-algebra}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.density_algebra}
\uses{def:densities}
\proved If $F'$ is obtained from $F$ by relabelling vertices or adding isolated vertices,
then $t(F',L)=t(F,L)$.  If $F_1,F_2$ have disjoint vertex sets, then
\[
 t(F_1\sqcup F_2,L)=t(F_1,L)t(F_2,L).
\]
If $L=L'$ a.e. and the kernels have a common finite bound, then $t(F,L)=t(F,L')$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A permutation of the coordinate factors preserves a product probability measure.  An
isolated coordinate contributes $\int1=1$.  Fubini separates the two disjoint vertex sets.
For the a.e. statement, each edge projection has the product measure on its two distinct
coordinates.  The preimage of the exceptional null set under that projection is null.
The union over the finitely many edges is null, so the products agree a.e.  Boundedness
justifies every integral and application of Fubini.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Complementation and parity expansion]
\label{lem:parity}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.colour_parity_expansion}
\uses{def:normalization,lem:density-algebra}
\proved Complementing $W$ replaces $U$ by $-U$ and leaves $M,A,R$ unchanged.  For any finite
edge set $E$ and fixed coordinates,
\[
 \frac12\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}\prod_{e\in E}(1+\sigma U_e)
 =\sum_{\substack{F\subseteq E\\|F|\ \mathrm{even}}}\prod_{e\in F}U_e,
\]
\[
 \frac12\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}\sigma\prod_{e\in E}(1+\sigma U_e)
 =\sum_{\substack{F\subseteq E\\|F|\ \mathrm{odd}}}\prod_{e\in F}U_e.
\]
In particular $m=\iint U$ can be assumed nonnegative after one complementation.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the finite product.  The coefficient of $\prod_{e\in F}U_e$ is the average of
$\sigma^{|F|}$, respectively $\sigma^{|F|+1}$.  These averages are $1$ at the stated parity
and $0$ otherwise.  Complementation interchanges the two signs.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cauchy--Schwarz and moment monotonicity]
\label{lem:moment-basics}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.probability_moment_inequalities}
\proved Let $\nu$ be a probability measure and let the following functions be bounded and
measurable.  Then
\[
 \left|\int fg\,d\nu\right|^2
 \le\left(\int f^2\,d\nu\right)\left(\int g^2\,d\nu\right).
\]
For $X\ge0$ and real $1\le p\le q$,
\[
 \int X^q\,d\nu\ge\left(\int X^p\,d\nu\right)^{q/p}.
\]
For finitely many $x_i\ge0$ and $s\ge1$,
\[
 \sum_i x_i^s\le\left(\sum_i x_i\right)^s.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For Cauchy--Schwarz, if $\int g^2=0$ then $g=0$ a.e.  Otherwise substitute
$t=(\int fg)/(\int g^2)$ in $\int(f-tg)^2\ge0$ and multiply by $\int g^2$.
For the moment inequality apply Jensen to $Y=X^p$ and the convex function $y\mapsto y^{q/p}$.
Here is the scalar justification, including the boundary.  For $s>1$ and $z>0$, the derivative
$s y^{s-1}$ is nondecreasing on $(0,\infty)$, so integration of the derivative gives
\[
 y^s\ge z^s+s z^{s-1}(y-z)\qquad(y\ge0).
\]
Take $z=\int Y$ and integrate.  If $z=0$, nonnegativity gives $Y=0$ a.e.; if $s=1$, the claim
is equality.  This proves the required Jensen instance without a strict-positivity assumption
on $X$.  Finally, if $S=\sum_i x_i>0$, then $0\le x_i/S\le1$ and
$\sum_i(x_i/S)^s\le\sum_i x_i/S=1$.  Multiply by $S^s$.  The case $S=0$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Two-coordinate power comparison]
\label{lem:pair-majorization}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.two_coordinate_power_comparison}
\uses{lem:moment-basics}
\proved Suppose $L_1,L_2,r_1,r_2\ge0$,
\[
 L_1+L_2\ge r_1+r_2,\qquad
 \max(L_1,L_2)\ge\max(r_1,r_2).
\]
Then $L_1^s+L_2^s\ge r_1^s+r_2^s$ for every real $s\ge1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Sort both pairs decreasingly as $(L_h,L_l)$ and $(r_h,r_l)$.  If $L_l\ge r_l$, use
termwise monotonicity.  Otherwise put $d=r_l-L_l$, so $0<d\le r_l$ and
$L_h\ge r_h+d$.  For $0\le t<d$ and $s>1$,
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}\bigl((r_h+t)^s+(r_l-t)^s\bigr)
 =s\bigl((r_h+t)^{s-1}-(r_l-t)^{s-1}\bigr)\ge0.
\]
Continuity includes $t=d$, also when $r_l-d=0$.  Thus
$(r_h+d)^s+(r_l-d)^s\ge r_h^s+r_l^s$.  Increasing $r_h+d$ to $L_h$ proves the result.
At $s=1$ use the total-sum hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Length lifting from two fourth moments]
\label{lem:length-lifting}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.length_lifting_two_fourth_moments}
\uses{lem:pair-majorization,lem:moment-basics}
\proved Let $V\ge0$ be bounded on a probability space.  Let $r_+,r_-\ge0$, and let $\omega$
be measurable with $0\le\omega\le2$ a.e. and $\E\omega=1$.  Suppose
\[
 \E V^4\ge\frac{r_++r_-}{2},\qquad
 \E\omega V^4\ge\max(r_+,r_-).
\]
For every real $p\ge4$,
\[
 \E V^p\ge\frac{r_+^{p/4}+r_-^{p/4}}2.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $L_+=\E\omega V^4$ and $L_-=\E(2-\omega)V^4$.  They are nonnegative, their sum is
$2\E V^4$, and $L_+\ge\max(r_+,r_-)$.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pair-majorization} with
$s=p/4$.  Both measures $\omega\,d\nu$ and $(2-\omega)\,d\nu$ have total mass one.
Jensen under each measure gives
\[
 \E V^p
 =\frac12\bigl(\E\omega(V^4)^s+\E(2-\omega)(V^4)^s\bigr)
 \ge\frac12(L_+^s+L_-^s)
 \ge\frac12(r_+^s+r_-^s).
\]
No division by $L_+$ or $L_-$ is used, so zero weighted moments are allowed.
\end{proof}

\section{A complete finite certificate language}
\label{sec:certificate-language}

This section separates the finite arithmetic assertions from their mathematical
interpretation.  It also specifies a direct route for checking the certificates inside Lean.
There is no appeal to a numerical semidefinite solver.

\begin{definition}[Six-vertex masks and graph polynomials]
\label{def:graph-polynomial}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.GraphPolynomial}
\uses{def:densities}
Let
\[
 \mathcal E_6=((0,1),(0,2),\ldots,(0,5),(1,2),\ldots,(4,5))
\]
be the lexicographically ordered list of the fifteen unordered pairs in $\Fin(6)$.
The position of $(i,j)$, for $i<j$, is
\[
 \iota(i,j)=\frac{i(11-i)}2+(j-i-1).
\]
A mask $g\in\Mask:=\{0,\ldots,2^{15}-1\}$ specifies the graph containing the edges at its
set bits.  Denote the formal basis vector for this graph by $[g]$.  A graph polynomial is a
vector $P=(P_g)_{g\in\Mask}\in\Q^{\Mask}$, evaluated by
\[
 \eval_U(P)=\sum_{g\in\Mask}P_g\,t(g,U).
\]
Graphs with fewer than six vertices are padded with isolated vertices.  If two masks have
disjoint edge sets, their labelled product is $[g]\cdot[h]=[g\cup h]$, extended bilinearly
when every relevant pair has disjoint edges.  This product is not used when an edge repeats.
\end{definition}

Padding with isolated vertices does not change a density by Lemma~\ref{lem:density-algebra}.
This is a formal graph algebra, not an algebra of injective embeddings.  Distinct formal
vertices can take the same value in a finite host, but this does not change the definition.

\begin{definition}[Parity polynomials and the four exact targets]
\label{def:certificate-targets}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.CertificateTargets}
\uses{def:graph-polynomial}
For a set $E$ of distinct formal edges and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$, write
\[
 \mathsf P_\epsilon(E)=
 \sum_{\substack{F\subseteq E\\ |F|\equiv\epsilon\ (2)}}[F].
\]
For $s\in\{2,3\}$ put $I_s=\{s,s+1,s+2\}$ and
\[
 E_s=\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<s,\ j\in I_s\}\cup\{\{s,s+1\},\{s,s+2\}\},
\]
\[
 B_s=\{\{i,j\}:0\le i<s,\ j\in\{s+1,s+2\}\}.
\]
The first two targets are
\[
 P_{\mathrm{mean},s}=\mathsf P_0(E_s)-\mathsf P_0(B_s),\qquad s=2,3.
\]
For the other two targets define
\[
 F_\epsilon=2\mathsf P_\epsilon(E_3)-\mathsf P_\epsilon(B_3),
 \quad
 P_\triangle=[01]+[02]+[12]-[01,02,12],
\]
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C&=\mathsf P_0(\{01,12,23,03\}),& M&=[01],& T_\triangle&=[01,02,12],\\
 A&=[01,23],& M T_\triangle&=[01,23,24,34],& P_3&=[01,12,23].
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $ij$ denotes $\{i,j\}$.  The symbol $M T_\triangle$ in the second line means the specified
disjoint-union graph, not overlapping multiplication of the earlier labelled masks.
Finally set
\begin{align*}
 P_-={}&3F_0-3C+F_1-P_\triangle\cdot F_0
       -13M-T_\triangle-12A+4MT_\triangle-12P_3,\\
 P_+={}&6F_0-6C+F_1+P_\triangle\cdot F_0
       -19M-23T_\triangle+12A-4MT_\triangle-24P_3.
\end{align*}
The multiplication $P_\triangle\cdot F_0$ is legal: every edge of $P_\triangle$ has both
ends in $\{0,1,2\}$ and no edge in $E_3$ or $B_3$ does.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Root types and rooted features]
\label{def:rooted-features}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.rootedFeature}
\uses{def:densities}
Choose $r$ labelled roots, $k$ further formal vertices, and a simple graph $F$ on these
$r+k$ vertices with no root--root edges.  For $\mathbf z\in\Omega^r$ define
\[
 \Phi_F(\mathbf z)=\int_{\Omega^k}
                  \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(F)}U(x_i,x_j)\,d\lambda^k,
\]
where $x_i=z_i$ for $i<r$.  For a literal root type $t\subseteq\binom{\Fin(r)}2$, put
\[
 p_t(\mathbf z)=2^{-\binom r2}
     \prod_{e\in t}(1+U_e)\prod_{e\notin t}(1-U_e).
\]
For a finite feature vector $\Phi$ and a rational symmetric matrix $Q$ of the same dimension,
write
\[
 \mathcal I_{r,t,\Phi,Q}(U)
 =\int_{\Omega^r}p_t(\mathbf z)\,
                  \Phi(\mathbf z)^{\mathsf T}Q\Phi(\mathbf z)\,d\lambda^r.
\]
The zero-fold product space has one point of mass one; these definitions include $r=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Rooted quadratic forms are nonnegative]
\label{lem:rooted-positivity}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.rooted_quadratic_nonnegative}
\uses{def:rooted-features}
\proved If $|U|\le1$ and $Q$ is positive semidefinite over $\R$, then
$\mathcal I_{r,t,\Phi,Q}(U)\ge0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fubini gives measurable representatives for the rooted features, and $|\Phi_F|\le1$ a.e.
Every factor $(1\pm U_e)/2$ lies in $[0,1]$, so $p_t\ge0$.  At every point where these
representatives are defined, $\Phi^{\mathsf T}Q\Phi\ge0$.  The integrand is bounded by the
finite sum of the absolute values of the entries of $Q$, and is integrable.  Its integral is
nonnegative.  On a finite host these statements are finite sums and pointwise inequalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Rational factorization implies positivity]
\label{lem:ldl-soundness}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.positive_diagonal_factorization_sound}
\proved Let $A$ be a $d\times d$ symmetric integer matrix and let $\denom>0$ be an integer.
Suppose rational data $L,\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_{d-1}$ satisfy
\[
 A=L\diag(\delta_0,\ldots,\delta_{d-1})L^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad L_{ii}=1,\quad L_{ij}=0\ (i<j),\quad\delta_i>0.
\]
Then $Q=A/\denom$ is positive definite, and hence positive semidefinite, as a real matrix.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Coercion $\Q\to\R$ preserves the finite matrix identity and strict inequalities.  For every
real vector $x$,
\[
 x^{\mathsf T}Qx=
 \frac1{\denom}\sum_i\delta_i\bigl((L^{\mathsf T}x)_i\bigr)^2\ge0.
\]
If the sum is zero, every coordinate of $L^{\mathsf T}x$ is zero.  Backward substitution in
the upper triangular matrix $L^{\mathsf T}$, whose diagonal entries are one, gives $x=0$.
Thus the quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Expansion of a rooted quadratic form]
\label{lem:rooted-expansion}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.rooted_quadratic_expansion}
\uses{def:graph-polynomial,def:rooted-features,lem:density-algebra}
\proved Suppose $r\le4$ and $r+2k\le6$.  Let $F_i'$ be a copy of $F_i$ obtained by moving its nonroot
vertices to $r+k,\ldots,r+2k-1$, while keeping its roots fixed.  If $Q=A/\denom$, then
\[
 64\denom\,\mathcal I_{r,t,\Phi,Q}(U)
 =\eval_U\left(
 2^{6-\binom r2}\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}
 \sum_{T\subseteq\binom{\Fin(r)}2}
 (-1)^{|T\setminus t|}[T\cup E(F_i)\cup E(F_j')]
 \right).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In $\Phi_{F_i}\Phi_{F_j}$ introduce independent copies of the $k$ integrated variables.
Fubini identifies the product with the density of the graph whose two extensions share
only the roots.  The extension graphs have no root--root edges, and their nonroot sets are
disjoint.  Consequently no edge is repeated.  Expand the finite product defining $p_t$;
a chosen root edge has coefficient $-1$ exactly when it is outside $t$.  The denominator is
$2^{\binom r2}\denom$.  Multiplication by $64\denom$ gives the factor
$2^{6-\binom r2}$.  All blocks used below have $r\le4$, so this factor is an integer.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The literal nineteen blocks}
The following list fixes the order of all matrix entries.  Root edges are always in
lexicographic order, with the first edge at bit zero.

\begin{definition}[Certificate feature schema]
\label{def:feature-schema}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.CertificateFeatureSchema}
\uses{def:rooted-features}
The nineteen blocks $(r,t,k,\Phi)$ are as follows.

For $r=0,k=3$, use the features with edge sets
$\{01\}$, $\{01,02\}$, and $\{01,02,12\}$, in that order.

For $r=1,k=2$ use the unique root type.  For $r=2,k=2$ use root types $t=0,1$ in that
order.  In both cases order the possible free edges as
\[
 (0,r),(0,r+1),(1,r),(1,r+1),\ldots,(r-1,r),(r-1,r+1),(r,r+1).
\]
Enumerate nonempty subsets by increasing binary mask, retaining a mask precisely when it
is at most the mask obtained by interchanging $r$ and $r+1$.  This gives $5$ features for
$r=1$ and $19$ for $r=2$.

For $r=3,k=1$ use root types $0,1,3,7$, in that order.  For $r=4,k=1$ use root types
\[
 0,1,3,7,11,12,13,15,30,31,63,
\]
in that order.  In each of these blocks the features are every nonempty subset of
$\{(i,r):0\le i<r\}$ in increasing binary-mask order.
\end{definition}

The dimensions of the blocks are
\[
 3,5,19,19,\underbrace{7,7,7,7}_{4},
 \underbrace{15,15,15,15,15,15,15,15,15,15,15}_{11}.
\]
There is no constant feature.  A feature list need not span a prescribed space for the
positivity argument: its entries and the coefficient identities alone matter.  In
particular, no completeness theorem about flag algebras is needed.

\begin{definition}[The integer data]
\label{def:certificate-data}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.CertificateData}
\uses{def:certificate-targets,def:feature-schema}
Set
\[
 \denom=90315258984881964711936.
\]
The four ordered collections of nineteen integer matrices are the files
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Target & Matrix collection\\\midrule
$P_{\mathrm{mean},2}$ & \code{mean_two_sos.json}\\
$P_{\mathrm{mean},3}$ & \code{mean_three_sos.json}\\
$P_-$ & \code{negative_majority_sos.json}\\
$P_+$ & \code{positive_majority_sos.json}\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Every matrix entry is the exact decimal integer in the corresponding file, divided by
$\denom$ when used as a rational quadratic-form coefficient.  All four files are embedded
verbatim in the standalone source.  The literal definitions in
\code{lean-data/CertificateData.lean} contain the same integer numerators.
\end{definition}

\subsection{The exact propositions to check}

A relabelling certificate consists of a function $\normform:\Mask\to\Mask$ and, for each
mask $g$, a permutation $\pi_g\in\Perm(\Fin(6))$ such that
$\pi_g\cdot g=\normform(g)$.  Extend $[g]\mapsto[\normform(g)]$ linearly to a map
$\mathsf N$ on graph polynomials.  The function need not be proved to give minimal or
unique isomorphism representatives.

\begin{lemma}[Soundness of coefficient grouping]
\label{lem:normalform-soundness}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.graph_normalization_sound}
\uses{def:graph-polynomial,lem:density-algebra}
\proved Suppose the stated permutation witnesses are valid.  If
$\mathsf N(P)=\mathsf N(Q)$ coefficientwise in $\Q^{\Mask}$, then
$\eval_U(P)=\eval_U(Q)$ for every bounded symmetric kernel.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Relabelling invariance gives $t(g,U)=t(\normform(g),U)$ separately for every $g$.  Replacing
each summand in the finite sum defining $\eval_U(P)$ proves
$\eval_U(P)=\eval_U(\mathsf N(P))$.  Apply the same argument to $Q$ and use the coefficient
identity.  No linear independence of graph densities is assumed.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Finite arithmetic assertions for all four certificates]
\label{prop:checked-data}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.all_certificate_checks}
\uses{def:certificate-data,def:feature-schema,def:certificate-targets}
\proved The following finite assertions hold for the literal data in
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-data}.

First, each of the $76$ matrices is symmetric and has a rational factorization of the form
in Lemma~\ref{lem:ldl-soundness}, with every diagonal factor strictly positive.
Second, there are valid permutation witnesses for all $32768$ masks.  Third, for each of
the four targets $P$,
\[
 \mathsf N(64\denom P)=
 \mathsf N\left(\sum_{j=1}^{19}2^{6-\binom{r_j}2}
 \sum_{a,b}(A_j)_{ab}\sum_{T\subseteq\binom{\Fin(r_j)}2}
 (-1)^{|T\setminus t_j|}[T\cup E(F_{j,a})\cup E(F'_{j,b})]\right).
 \tag{C}
\]
Equality holds in all $32768$ coefficient positions, including positions where both sides
are zero.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
These are finite rational assertions about fully specified integers.  The source verifier
recomputes the targets from Definition~\ref{def:certificate-targets}, recomputes the rooted
expansions from Definition~\ref{def:feature-schema}, groups by all six-vertex isomorphisms,
and checks every coefficient and every leading principal minor.

A second implementation, \code{independent_audit.py}, does not import either source
checker.  It constructs relabelling witnesses by breadth-first search using the five adjacent
vertex transpositions.  Each of the resulting $32768$ witnesses is then checked by applying
its explicit permutation to its mask.  It constructs the parity and type polynomials by
successive convolution, rather than by the source checker's subset routine.  It checks (C)
in all coefficient positions for each of the four targets.

For positivity, the second implementation constructs rational $L,\delta$ by
\[
 \delta_j=A_{jj}-\sum_{h<j}L_{jh}^2\delta_h,
 \qquad
 L_{ij}=\frac{A_{ij}-\sum_{h<j}L_{ih}\delta_hL_{jh}}{\delta_j}\quad(i>j),
\]
starting with unit diagonal $L$.  It checks $\delta_j>0$ before division, and then independently
checks every entry of $L\diag(\delta)L^{\mathsf T}=A$.  There are $956$ positive rational
pivots and $13708$ matrix-entry equalities.  The factors are supplied in
\code{ldl_witnesses.json}; recomputing them from the integer matrices is also possible.

Both complete arithmetic checks succeeded.  Their sources, exact data, and complete
outputs accompany this blueprint.  This is the conventional finite verification of the
proposition.  In Lean, (C), the permutation equations, the triangular-factor equations, and
the positive rational signs must be closed decidable goals, as specified in
Section~\ref{sec:lean-plan}.  No statement that this Lean step has already been completed
is intended.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Four universal polynomial inequalities]
\label{thm:certificate-inequalities}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.four_universal_graph_inequalities}
\uses{prop:checked-data,lem:normalform-soundness,lem:rooted-expansion,lem:ldl-soundness,lem:rooted-positivity}
\proved For every probability space and every symmetric measurable $U$ with $|U|\le1$,
\[
 \eval_U(P_{\mathrm{mean},2})\ge0,\quad
 \eval_U(P_{\mathrm{mean},3})\ge0,\quad
 \eval_U(P_-)\ge0,\quad
 \eval_U(P_+)\ge0.
\]
No condition on the sign of $\iint U$ is needed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:normalform-soundness} to (C).  Divide by the positive integer
$64\denom$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:rooted-expansion}.  Each target is exactly the sum of its
nineteen rooted quadratic-form integrals.  Each integral is nonnegative by
Lemmas~\ref{lem:ldl-soundness} and~\ref{lem:rooted-positivity}.
\end{proof}

\section{Finite kernels and the required spectral facts}
\label{sec:finite-spectral}

Throughout Sections~\ref{sec:finite-spectral}--\ref{sec:finite-completion}, fix an integer
$d\ge1$ and a real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix $U$ with $|U_{ij}|\le1$.  The host probability
space is $\Fin(d)$ with each point of mass $1/d$.  Its diagonal entries are allowed and are
not deleted.  They correspond to within-cell values of a step graphon, not to formal loops
in the graphs whose densities are being counted.

\begin{definition}[Normalized matrix operator and scalar moments]
\label{def:finite-scalars}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.scalars}
\uses{def:densities,def:normalization}
On $\R^d$ use the inner product
\[
 \inner{x}{y}_d=\frac1d\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_i y_i.
\]
Let $\one$ be the all-ones vector; its norm is one.  Define
\[
 (Tx)_i=\frac1d\sum_jU_{ij}x_j,\qquad
 f=T\one,\qquad m=\inner{\one}{f}_d,\qquad a=m^2,\qquad b=\inner f f_d.
\]
Set
\[
 c=\Tr T^4,\quad r=c^{1/4},\quad v=b-a,\quad
 p_3=\inner{\one}{T^3\one}_d,\quad\tau=\tau_3=\Tr T^3.
\]
The codegree matrix is
\[
 K_{ij}=\frac1d\sum_t U_{it}U_{jt}.
\]
As a normalized kernel operator it is $T^2$.  Put $L_0=U\cdot K$, a pointwise product.
Write $T_{S_\sigma}=S_\sigma/d$ and $r_{\sigma,4}=\Tr T_{S_\sigma}^4$.
\end{definition}

\paragraph{Implementation of the normalization.}
The isometry from this inner-product space to ordinary Euclidean $\R^d$ is
$x\mapsto x/\sqrt d$.  The matrix of $T$ remains $U/d$ under this isometry, while the unit
constant vector becomes $(1/\sqrt d,\ldots,1/\sqrt d)$.  A Lean implementation can use this
ordinary Euclidean model.  It must not treat the unnormalized all-ones vector as a Euclidean
unit vector.

\begin{lemma}[Finite symmetric spectral theorem and trace bounds]
\label{lem:finite-spectral}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.spectral_trace_bounds}
\uses{lem:moment-basics}
\proved A real symmetric $d\times d$ matrix $B$ has real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis.  For every integer $q\ge1$,
\[
 \Tr B^q=\sum_i\lambda_i^q,\qquad
 \|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_i|\lambda_i|.
\]
For every even integer $n\ge4$ and every unit vector $g$,
\[
 \Tr B^n\ge\|Bg\|^n,\qquad
 \Tr B^n\ge|\inner g{Bg}|^n,
 \qquad
 \Tr B^n\le(\Tr B^4)^{n/4}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For completeness, diagonalization follows by induction on dimension.  The quadratic form
$x\mapsto\inner x{Bx}$ attains a maximum on the unit sphere.  At a maximizing unit vector
$u$, differentiating along $(u+tv)/\|u+tv\|$ for $v\perp u$ gives
$\inner v{Bu}=0$.  Thus $Bu$ is a scalar multiple of $u$.  Symmetry makes $u^\perp$
invariant, and induction gives an orthonormal eigenbasis there.  The dimension-one case
is immediate.  This is the standard finite-dimensional real symmetric spectral theorem;
a formalization may use its library version.

In the eigenbasis, trace and operator norm have the stated expressions.  Since $n$ is even,
$\sum_i\lambda_i^n=\sum_i|\lambda_i|^n\ge\max_i|\lambda_i|^n$.
The unit-vector inequalities follow from $\|Bg\|\le\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and
$|\inner g{Bg}|\le\|Bg\|$.  For the upper bound apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:moment-basics} to $x_i=|\lambda_i|^4$ and $s=n/4\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cycle trace identity]
\label{lem:cycle-trace}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.cycle_trace}
\uses{def:finite-scalars,def:densities}
\proved For a symmetric finite kernel $L$ and integer $n\ge3$,
\[
 t(C_n,L)=\Tr(L/d)^n.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The trace expansion is
\[
 \Tr(L/d)^n
 =d^{-n}\sum_{i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1}}
 L_{i_0i_1}L_{i_1i_2}\cdots L_{i_{n-1}i_0}.
\]
This is exactly the uniform average in Definition~\ref{def:densities}.  Each formal vertex
is a different coordinate of the sum, even when some host values coincide.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Basic scalar bounds]
\label{lem:scalar-bounds}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.basic_scalar_bounds}
\uses{def:finite-scalars,lem:finite-spectral,lem:cycle-trace,lem:moment-basics}
\proved After complementation so that $m\ge0$,
\[
 0\le m\le1,\quad 0\le a\le b\le1,\quad 0\le c\le1,\quad
 0\le r\le1,\quad\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le r,\quad |p_3|\le br.
\]
Also $c=d^{-2}\sum_{i,j}K_{ij}^2$, and $c=0$ if and only if every entry of $U$ is zero.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every $f_i$ is an average of numbers in $[-1,1]$, hence $b\le1$ and $|m|\le1$.
Cauchy--Schwarz at the unit constant vector gives $a\le b$.  Symmetry gives
\[
 \Tr T^2=d^{-2}\sum_{i,j}U_{ij}^2\le1.
\]
If $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $T$, then
\[
 c=\sum_i\lambda_i^4\le\left(\sum_i\lambda_i^2\right)^2\le1,
 \qquad \|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\le c.
\]
Taking nonnegative fourth roots gives the bounds for $r$.  Self-adjointness yields
$p_3=\inner f{Tf}_d$, so $|p_3|\le\|f\|^2\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le br$.
The matrix identity $T^2=K/d$ gives
$c=\Tr(T^2)^2=d^{-2}\sum K_{ij}^2$.  If $c=0$, every eigenvalue of $T$ is zero; symmetry
then gives $T=0$ and $U=0$.  The converse is immediate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The two fourth colour traces]
\label{lem:fourth-traces}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.fourth_colour_traces}
\uses{lem:parity,lem:cycle-trace,def:finite-scalars,lem:density-algebra}
\proved One has
\[
 R_4=1+2a+4b+c,\qquad
 r_{\sigma,4}=R_4+4\sigma(m+p_3).
\]
The formulas also hold for graphons when the scalar quantities are defined by their
corresponding integrals.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand the four factors $1+\sigma U$ around the four-cycle.  The edge-subset contributions
are
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cll@{}}
\toprule
Edges chosen & Multiplicity and graph & Contribution\\\midrule
0 & one empty subset & $1$\\
1 & four single edges & $4\sigma m$\\
2 & four adjacent pairs, two disjoint pairs & $4b+2a$\\
3 & four paths of length three & $4\sigma p_3$\\
4 & the entire cycle & $c$\\\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
There are $1+4+6+4+1=16$ subsets.  Disjoint unions and isolated vertices are treated by
Lemma~\ref{lem:density-algebra}.  Averaging the two colours gives the formula for $R_4$.
All steps are finite product expansions and Fubini, so the integral version is identical.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Even-cycle lower bound on finite kernels]
\label{lem:finite-even-cycle}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.even_cycle_lower_bound}
\uses{lem:finite-spectral,lem:cycle-trace,lem:parity,def:finite-scalars}
\proved For every even integer $n\ge4$,
\[
 R_n\ge\frac{(1+m)^n+(1-m)^n}{2}
 \ge1+\binom n2m^2\ge1.
\]
In particular $r_{-,4}\ge(1-m)^4$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The Rayleigh value of $T_{S_\sigma}$ at the unit vector $\one$ is $1+\sigma m\ge0$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-spectral} to each colour and average.  In the binomial
expansion, the odd powers of $m$ cancel and every even-power term is nonnegative.
Keep the terms of degree zero and two.  The coefficient $\binom n2$ is strictly positive.
\end{proof}

\section{Conditional second spectral moments}
\label{sec:conditional}

\begin{definition}[Conditional quantities for an arbitrary apex number]
\label{def:conditional}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.conditionalMoments}
\uses{def:finite-scalars}
Let $s\ge1$, choose a uniform sign and independent uniform apex coordinates
$\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_s)\in\Fin(d)^s$, and define
\[
 h_s(x)=\prod_{i=1}^s S_\sigma(z_i,x),\qquad D_s=\E_x h_s(x),
\]
\[
 A_s^{\mathrm{in}}(x)=\E_y S_\sigma(x,y)h_s(y),\quad
 N_s=\E_x h_s(x)A_s^{\mathrm{in}}(x),\quad
 \Pi_s=\E_x h_s(x)A_s^{\mathrm{in}}(x)^2.
\]
The superscript on $A_s^{\mathrm{in}}$ distinguishes this inner function from the normalized
apex density $A_{n/2,s}$.  In the note's operator notation,
$A_s^{\mathrm{in}}=T_{S_\sigma}h_s$.
Put
\[
 B_s=M_{\sqrt{h_s}}T_{S_\sigma}M_{\sqrt{h_s}},\qquad
 Q_s=\begin{cases}N_s/D_s&D_s>0,\\0&D_s=0,\end{cases}
\]
\[
 \QQ{s}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{\Pi_s/D_s}&D_s>0,\\0&D_s=0.\end{cases}
\]
Unsubscripted expectations in the conditional argument average both the sign and all
apices.  Inner expectations $\E_x,\E_y$ average only their stated coordinates.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Bounds and zero denominators]
\label{lem:conditional-bounds}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.conditional_bounds}
\uses{def:conditional,lem:moment-basics}
\proved Pointwise in the colour and apices,
\[
 0\le h_s\le2^s,\quad 0\le D_s\le2^s,\quad
 0\le A_s^{\mathrm{in}}\le2D_s,\quad
 0\le\Pi_s\le4D_s^3.
\]
If $D_s=0$, then $h_s=0$ at every host point and $N_s=\Pi_s=B_s=0$.
Also
\[
 0\le Q_s\le\QQ{s}\le2D_s\le2^{s+1},\qquad
 D_s(\QQ{s})^2=\Pi_s.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every factor of $h_s$ is in $[0,2]$.  Averaging gives the first two bounds.  Since
$S_\sigma\le2$, $A_s^{\mathrm{in}}\le2D_s$, and hence
$\Pi_s\le\E_x h_s(x)4D_s^2=4D_s^3$.  If the nonnegative average $D_s$ is zero, every
$h_s(x)$ is zero because each host atom has positive mass.  This proves all zero statements.
For $D_s>0$, use the probability measure with masses $h_s(x)/(dD_s)$ and apply
Cauchy--Schwarz to its first and second moments of $A_s^{\mathrm{in}}$.  This gives
$Q_s^2\le\Pi_s/D_s$.  The upper bound follows from $\Pi_s/D_s\le4D_s^2$.
The final identity follows from the definition when $D_s>0$ and from $\Pi_s=0$ otherwise.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Unit vector and retained variance]
\label{lem:conditional-vector}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.conditional_vector_identity}
\uses{def:conditional,lem:conditional-bounds}
\proved If $D_s>0$, then $g_s=\sqrt{h_s}/\sqrt{D_s}$ is a unit vector in the normalized
inner product and
\[
 \inner{g_s}{B_sg_s}_d=Q_s,\qquad
 \|B_sg_s\|_d^2=\frac{\Pi_s}{D_s}=(\QQ{s})^2.
\]
Moreover
\[
 (\QQ{s})^2-Q_s^2
 =\E_x\frac{h_s(x)}{D_s}\bigl(A_s^{\mathrm{in}}(x)-Q_s\bigr)^2\ge0.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The squared norm of $g_s$ is $D_s/D_s=1$.  Direct multiplication gives
\[
 (B_sg_s)(x)=\frac{\sqrt{h_s(x)}}{\sqrt{D_s}}A_s^{\mathrm{in}}(x).
\]
Taking the inner product with $g_s$ and then taking its squared norm proves the two
identities.  For the variance expand the square, use
$\E_x h_s/D_s=1$ and $\E_x h_sA_s^{\mathrm{in}}/D_s=Q_s$, and simplify.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Conditional trace representation and spectral bound]
\label{prop:conditional-trace}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.conditional_trace_bound}
\uses{lem:conditional-vector,lem:conditional-bounds,lem:finite-spectral,lem:cycle-trace,def:normalization}
\proved For every even $n\ge4$ and every $s\ge1$,
\[
 A_{n/2,s}=\E\Tr B_s^n\ge\E(\QQ{s})^n.
\]
This is the strengthening of the note's conditional representation (9) used in
Proposition~2.1 of \sourceuniversal.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Expand the matrix trace:
\[
 \Tr B_s^n=d^{-n}\sum_{x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}}
 \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}S_\sigma(x_j,x_{j+1})\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}h_s(x_j),
 \qquad x_n=x_0.
\]
At each formal cycle coordinate, two factors $\sqrt{h_s(x_j)}$ multiply to $h_s(x_j)$.
Averaging the $s$ apices introduces exactly their $ns$ incident edges.  Averaging the
colour and using Definition~\ref{def:normalization} gives the equality.
For $D_s>0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-spectral} at $g_s$ gives
$\Tr B_s^n\ge\|B_sg_s\|^n=(\QQ{s})^n$.  For $D_s=0$, both are zero.
The matrix $B_s$ is symmetric, but it is not required to be positive semidefinite.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Polynomial support and a global Cauchy--Schwarz bound]
\label{lem:quartic-support}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.sharp_fourth_support}
\uses{lem:conditional-bounds,lem:moment-basics}
\proved For every $s\ge1$,
\[
 (\QQ{s})^4\ge2\Pi_s-D_s^2.
\]
If $Z_s=\E D_s^2>0$, then
\[
 \E(\QQ{s})^4\ge\frac{(\E\Pi_s)^2}{Z_s}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For $D_s>0$, the exact identity is
\[
 (\QQ{s})^4-(2\Pi_s-D_s^2)=\left(\frac{\Pi_s}{D_s}-D_s\right)^2.
\]
For $D_s=0$, all terms vanish.  The second assertion follows from
\[
 (\E\Pi_s)^2=\bigl(\E D_s(\QQ{s})^2\bigr)^2
 \le (\E D_s^2)\E(\QQ{s})^4.
\]
Division is used only after the hypothesis $Z_s>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Codegree powers and the two small-graph identities]
\label{lem:codegree-moments}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.codegree_moment_identities}
\uses{def:conditional,def:certificate-targets,lem:parity,lem:cycle-trace,lem:moment-basics}
\proved Define $C_\sigma(x,y)=\E_zS_\sigma(x,z)S_\sigma(y,z)$.  Then
\[
 C_\sigma\ge0,\qquad
 Z_s:=\E D_s^2=\E_{\sigma,x,y}C_\sigma(x,y)^s,
 \qquad Z_2=R_4,\qquad Z_3\ge R_4^{3/2}.
\]
For $s=2,3$,
\[
 \E\Pi_s-Z_s=\eval_U(P_{\mathrm{mean},s}).
\]
Also the graph for $\E\Pi_s$ is $K_{1,2,s}$, and
\[
 \E\Pi_s=2^{3s+1}M(K_{1,2,s},W),\qquad
 Z_s=2^{2s-1}M(K_{2,s},W).
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Expand $D_s^2$ using two independent inner coordinates $x,y$.  Averaging each apex gives
a factor $C_\sigma(x,y)$, independently of the other apices.  The case $s=2$ is a four-cycle.
For $s=3$ apply the moment inequality to $C_\sigma$ on the probability space of one colour
and two host coordinates.

Expanding $\Pi_s$ introduces three independent inner vertices.  Each is joined to all
$s$ apices, and the first inner vertex is joined to the other two.  The edge set is exactly
$E_s$ from Definition~\ref{def:certificate-targets}; the edge set for $D_s^2$ is $B_s$.
Apply the even-parity expansion.  The graph is complete tripartite with part sizes $1,2,s$;
it has $3s+2$ edges.  The graph for $Z_s$ has $2s$ edges.  Definition~\ref{def:normalization}
gives the two powers of $2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Three-apex polynomial lower expression]
\label{def:three-apex-polynomial}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.threeApexPolynomial}
\uses{def:conditional}
For three apices define
\[
 \FF=2\Pi_3-D_3^2,\qquad \JJ_0=\E\FF.
\]
The random variable $\FF$ may have either sign.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Unrestricted mean inequalities]
\label{cor:reference-mean}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.reference_mean_bounds}
\uses{thm:certificate-inequalities,lem:codegree-moments,lem:quartic-support,lem:finite-even-cycle,def:three-apex-polynomial}
\proved For every finite kernel,
\[
 \E\Pi_2\ge Z_2,\qquad \E\Pi_3\ge Z_3,\qquad
 \E(\QQ{2})^4\ge R_4.
\]
For three apices,
\[
 \E(\QQ{3})^4\ge\JJ_0\ge Z_3\ge R_4^{3/2}\ge R_4\ge1.
\]
The random variable $\FF$ is not required to be pointwise nonnegative.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The first two inequalities are Theorem~\ref{thm:certificate-inequalities} interpreted by
Lemma~\ref{lem:codegree-moments}.  Since $Z_2=R_4\ge1$, the global Cauchy--Schwarz bound
gives $\E(\QQ{2})^4\ge Z_2^2/Z_2=R_4$.  For three apices the pointwise support inequality
gives the first comparison.  Next,
$\JJ_0=2\E\Pi_3-Z_3\ge Z_3$.  The rest is
Lemma~\ref{lem:codegree-moments} and $R_4\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Scalar comparison and the global weighted fourth moment}
\label{sec:weighted}

The quantities $\FF$ and $\JJ_0$ in this section always use three apices.  Scalar $m$ is
assumed nonnegative, after complementation.  The two certificate inequalities used below
remain valid without that assumption.

\begin{lemma}[Fourth-cycle amplification]
\label{lem:amplification}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.fourth_cycle_amplification}
\uses{lem:fourth-traces,lem:scalar-bounds,cor:reference-mean}
\proved One has
\[
 R_4^{3/2}\ge R_4+4br.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $R=R_4$.  The formula $R=1+2a+4b+r^4$ gives $R\ge1$.
If $r\le1/2$, put $z=\sqrt R\ge1$.  Since
$2R-\sqrt R-1=(2z+1)(z-1)\ge0$,
\[
 R^{3/2}-R
 =\frac{R}{\sqrt R+1}(R-1)
 \ge\frac{R-1}{2}\ge2b\ge4br.
\]
Every denominator is positive.

Now suppose $r\ge1/2$.  The function $y^{3/2}-y$ is increasing for $y\ge1$: its derivative
is $3\sqrt y/2-1\ge1/2$.  It therefore suffices to replace $R$ by
$1+4b+r^4$.  Set $x=\sqrt{1+4b+r^4}$, so
$4br=r(x^2-1-r^4)$.  The required difference is
\[
 x^3-(1+r)x^2+r+r^5.
\]
For $A=1+r>0$, the identity
\[
 x^3-Ax^2+\frac{4A^3}{27}
 =\left(x-\frac{2A}{3}\right)^2\left(x+\frac A3\right)\ge0
\]
holds for $x\ge0$.  Hence the difference is at least
$r+r^5-4(1+r)^3/27$.  Put $t=r-1/2\ge0$.  Direct expansion gives
\begin{align*}
 27r^5-4r^3-12r^2+15r-4
 ={}&27t^5+\frac{135}{2}t^4+\frac{127}{2}t^3\\
 &+\frac{63}{4}t^2+\frac{135}{16}t+\frac{27}{32}>0.
\end{align*}
Dividing by $27$ proves the claim.  The rational expansion is also independently checked
by the auxiliary algebra program.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[An auxiliary nonnegative scalar]
\label{lem:auxiliary-D}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.auxiliary_scalar_nonnegative}
\uses{cor:reference-mean,lem:fourth-traces,lem:finite-even-cycle}
\proved The quantity
\[
 \DD=2\JJ_0-R_4-4p_3-1
\]
is nonnegative.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The negative-colour Rayleigh bound and the fourth-trace identity give
\begin{align*}
 R_4-4p_3
 &=r_{-,4}+4m\\
 &\ge(1-m)^4+4m\\
 &=1+m^2\bigl((m-2)^2+2\bigr)\ge1.
\end{align*}
Since $\JJ_0\ge R_4$,
$\DD=2(\JJ_0-R_4)+(R_4-4p_3-1)\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Majority polynomial and signed conditional moments]
\label{def:majority}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.majorityMoments}
\uses{def:conditional,cor:reference-mean}
For three apices define
\[
 \PP=U(z_1,z_2)+U(z_1,z_3)+U(z_2,z_3)
       -U(z_1,z_2)U(z_1,z_3)U(z_2,z_3),
\]
\[
 \mu=3m-\tau,\qquad
 \JJ_\sigma=\E\sigma\FF,\qquad
 \JJ_{\PP}=\E\PP\FF.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Bound and centering of the majority polynomial]
\label{lem:majority-bounds}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.majority_bound_and_mean}
\uses{def:majority,lem:cycle-trace,lem:density-algebra}
\proved One has $|\PP|\le2$ pointwise and $\E\PP=\mu$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $P(x,y,z)=x+y+z-xyz$.  For $(x,y,z)\in[-1,1]^3$, multiaffine interpolation gives
\[
 P(x,y,z)=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^3}P(\epsilon)
              \prod_{i=1}^3\frac{1+\epsilon_i x_i}{2},
 \qquad (x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x,y,z).
\]
The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.  If at least two entries of $\epsilon$ are
positive then $P(\epsilon)=2$; otherwise it is $-2$.  This proves the bound.
Each single edge in the apex triple has expectation $m$, and their triangular product has
expectation $t(C_3,U)=\tau$.  Thus $\E\PP=3m-\tau$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Interpretation of the two weighted certificates]
\label{lem:GH}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.weighted_certificate_inequalities}
\uses{thm:certificate-inequalities,def:certificate-targets,lem:codegree-moments,lem:parity,lem:density-algebra,def:majority,lem:fourth-traces}
\proved The following quantities are nonnegative:
\begin{align}
 G={}&3\JJ_0-3R_4+\JJ_\sigma-\JJ_{\PP}
       -13m-\tau-12a+4m\tau-12p_3\ge0,\label{eq:blueprint-G}\\
 H={}&6\JJ_0-6R_4+\JJ_\sigma+\JJ_{\PP}
       -19m-23\tau+12a-4m\tau-24p_3\ge0.\label{eq:blueprint-H}
\end{align}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By the conditional graph expansion,
$\eval_U(F_0)=\JJ_0$ and $\eval_U(F_1)=\JJ_\sigma$.  Multiplication by the root-only
polynomial $P_\triangle$ gives
$\eval_U(P_\triangle\cdot F_0)=\JJ_{\PP}$; no edge repeats.
The scalar mask evaluations in Definition~\ref{def:certificate-targets} are
\[
 \eval_U(C)=R_4,\quad \eval_U(M)=m,\quad
 \eval_U(T_\triangle)=\tau,\quad\eval_U(A)=m^2=a,
\]
\[
 \eval_U(MT_\triangle)=m\tau,\qquad\eval_U(P_3)=p_3.
\]
The disjoint-union interpretations of $a$ and $m\tau$ use
Lemma~\ref{lem:density-algebra}.  Substitution shows that $G=\eval_U(P_-)$ and
$H=\eval_U(P_+)$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:certificate-inequalities} proves their nonnegativity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Global weighted reference comparison]
\label{thm:weighted-reference}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.weighted_fourth_reference}
\uses{lem:majority-bounds,lem:GH,lem:auxiliary-D,lem:amplification,cor:reference-mean,lem:quartic-support,lem:fourth-traces,lem:scalar-bounds}
\proved For every finite kernel there exists a function $\omega$ of the colour and three
apices such that
\[
 0\le\omega\le2,\qquad\E\omega=1,\qquad
 \E\omega(\QQ{3})^4\ge\max(r_{+,4},r_{-,4}).
\]
After choosing the complement with $m\ge0$, the following formulas specify $\omega$
completely:
\[
 \omega=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&m+p_3\le0,\\[2pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{3+2\mu+\sigma-\PP}{3+\mu},
      &m+p_3>0\text{ and }\mu\ge0,\\[7pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{6-2\mu+\sigma+\PP}{6-\mu},
      &m+p_3>0\text{ and }\mu<0.
 \end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The three cases are disjoint and exhaustive.  The case decision is made from scalar
moments of the kernel, not from the sampled colour or apex coordinates.

\paragraph{Case 1: $m+p_3\le0$.}
The constant density is admissible.  Since $m\ge0$, we have $p_3\le-m\le0$ and
$-(m+p_3)\le|p_3|\le br$.  Thus
\[
 \E(\QQ{3})^4\ge\JJ_0\ge R_4^{3/2}\ge R_4+4br
 \ge R_4-4(m+p_3)=r_{-,4}.
\]
By the trace formula this is the larger of the two fourth traces.

\paragraph{Case 2: $m+p_3>0$ and $\mu\ge0$.}
Put $d_-=3+\mu>0$ and $\omega_-=(3+2\mu+\sigma-\PP)/d_-$.
Since $-3\le\sigma-\PP\le3$, its numerator lies between $2\mu$ and $6+2\mu=2d_-$.
It follows that $0\le\omega_-\le2$.  The mean of its numerator is
$3+2\mu+0-\mu=3+\mu$, so $\E\omega_-=1$.
Multiplying the pointwise bound $(\QQ{3})^4\ge\FF$ by this nonnegative density gives
\begin{align*}
 d_-\bigl(\E\omega_-(\QQ{3})^4-r_{+,4}\bigr)
 &\ge(3+2\mu)\JJ_0+\JJ_\sigma-\JJ_{\PP}
                 -(3+\mu)(R_4+4m+4p_3)\\
 &=G+4m+\mu\DD\ge0.
\end{align*}
The equality is a polynomial identity after inserting
$\mu=3m-\tau$, $a=m^2$, and the definitions of $G,\DD$.
Every term in the last expression is nonnegative.  Divide by $d_->0$.
Since $m+p_3>0$, the larger trace is $r_{+,4}$.

\paragraph{Case 3: $m+p_3>0$ and $\mu<0$.}
Put $d_+=6-\mu>0$ and $\omega_+=(6-2\mu+\sigma+\PP)/d_+$.
Its numerator lies between $3-2\mu>0$ and $9-2\mu\le12-2\mu=2d_+$.
Its expectation is $6-2\mu+0+\mu=d_+$.  Thus it is again admissible.
The other polynomial identity gives
\begin{align*}
 d_+\bigl(\E\omega_+(\QQ{3})^4-r_{+,4}\bigr)
 &\ge(6-2\mu)\JJ_0+\JJ_\sigma+\JJ_{\PP}
                 -(6-\mu)(R_4+4m+4p_3)\\
 &=H+24\tau-8m-\mu\DD.
\end{align*}
Now $\tau>3m\ge0$, so $24\tau-8m\ge0$, and $-\mu\DD\ge0$.
The last expression is nonnegative.  Divide by $d_+>0$.
The larger trace is again $r_{+,4}$.

If the original kernel had negative mean, perform the construction for $-U$ and interchange
the two colour labels.  The law of the conditional quantity and the unordered pair of
base traces are unchanged.  This provides a density on the original sampling space too.
\end{proof}

\section{Completion on all finite uniform kernels}
\label{sec:finite-completion}

\begin{theorem}[Three-apex relative inequality at every even length]
\label{thm:finite-three}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.three_apex_relative}
\uses{thm:weighted-reference,cor:reference-mean,lem:length-lifting,prop:conditional-trace,lem:finite-spectral,lem:cycle-trace}
\proved For every finite symmetric kernel in $[-1,1]$ and every even $n\ge4$,
\[
 A_{n/2,3}\ge R_n.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:length-lifting} to $V=\QQ3$ and $r_\pm=r_{\pm,4}$.
The mean condition is Corollary~\ref{cor:reference-mean}, and the weighted condition is
Theorem~\ref{thm:weighted-reference}.  Consequently
\begin{align*}
 A_{n/2,3}
 &\ge\E(\QQ3)^n\\
 &\ge\frac12\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}(r_{\sigma,4})^{n/4}\\
 &\ge\frac12\sum_{\sigma=\pm1}\Tr T_{S_\sigma}^{n}=R_n.
\end{align*}
The penultimate inequality is the upper trace bound in Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-spectral}
applied separately to the two base-colour matrices.  This argument includes $n=4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Apex-number lifting, with exact normalization]
\label{lem:apex-lifting}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.apex_number_moment_lifting}
\uses{def:normalization,lem:moment-basics,lem:density-algebra}
\proved On any probability space where the densities are defined, suppose $R_n>0$.
For integers $k\ge s\ge1$,
\[
 A_{n/2,k}\ge\frac{A_{n/2,s}^{k/s}}{R_n^{k/s-1}}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
On the probability space of a uniform colour and $n$ independent base vertices, define
\[
 b_n(\sigma,\mathbf x)=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}S_\sigma(x_i,x_{i+1}),\quad x_n=x_0,
 \qquad
 \xi(\sigma,\mathbf x)=\int\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}S_\sigma(z,x_i)\,d\lambda(z).
\]
Both functions are nonnegative and bounded by $2^n$.  Let $\nu$ be the finite measure with
density $b_n$ with respect to that product probability measure.  Fubini gives
\[
 \nu(\Omega')=R_n,\qquad \int\xi^j\,d\nu=A_{n/2,j}\quad(j\ge1).
\]
The reason is that $j$ independent new vertices contribute $j$ separate copies of $\xi$,
and no edges among them.  Dividing $\nu$ by its positive mass $R_n$ gives a probability
measure.  Jensen at exponent $k/s\ge1$, applied to $\xi^s$, yields
\[
 \frac{A_{n/2,k}}{R_n}
 \ge\left(\frac{A_{n/2,s}}{R_n}\right)^{k/s}.
\]
Multiply by $R_n$ and use the rules for positive real powers.  This is exactly the note's
moment-lifting lemma, Lemma~2.3, with all normalizations expressed directly using $S_\sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Diamond identity and its lower bound]
\label{lem:diamond}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.diamond_lower_bound}
\uses{def:conditional,lem:parity,def:finite-scalars,lem:moment-basics,lem:density-algebra}
\proved For one apex,
\[
 Z_1=\E D_1^2=1+b,\qquad
 X:=\E\Pi_1=1+2a+8b+c+4q,
\]
where
\[
 q=\E_{x,y}f(x)U(x,y)K(x,y),\qquad |q|\le\sqrt{bc}.
\]
In particular,
\[
 X\ge1+2b+\frac c3.
\]
The same graph-density and integral identities hold for graphons.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For one apex, $D_1(z)=1+\sigma f(z)$; averaging its square over colour and $z$ gives $1+b$.
The graph for $\Pi_1$ is $K_{1,2,1}$, the diamond with five edges.  Its even edge subsets
have the following complete classification: one empty subset; two two-edge matchings and
eight adjacent two-edge pairs; one four-cycle and four triangles with a pendant edge.
They give $1$, $2a+8b$, and $c+4q$, respectively.  For the pendant-edge term, first integrate
its leaf, obtaining $f(x)$; integrate the remaining two edges from the third triangle vertex,
obtaining $K(x,y)$; the last edge is $U(x,y)$.  This proves the formula for $q$.

Cauchy--Schwarz on the pair space gives
\[
 |q|^2\le\E_{x,y}f(x)^2\,\E_{x,y}U(x,y)^2K(x,y)^2\le b c.
\]
Finally,
\begin{align*}
 X-1-2b-c/3
 &\ge2a+6b+2c/3-4\sqrt{bc}\\
 &=2a+\left(\sqrt{6b}-\sqrt{2c/3}\right)^2\ge0.
\end{align*}
The integral argument is identical, with Fubini justified by boundedness.  The identity is
also the two-apex moment identity (14) of the note: the same diamond is obtained by
integrating the inner vertex in the present representation.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-host theorem with the needed quantitative bounds]
\label{thm:finite-main}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.FiniteKernel.all_even_apex_bounds}
\uses{thm:finite-three,lem:apex-lifting,lem:finite-even-cycle,cor:reference-mean,prop:conditional-trace,lem:quartic-support,lem:diamond,lem:moment-basics}
\proved For every $d\ge1$, every symmetric $U\in[-1,1]^{d\times d}$, every even $n\ge4$,
and every integer $k\ge1$,
\begin{align*}
 A_{n/2,1}&\ge\left(\frac{X^2}{1+b}\right)^{n/4}\ge1,\\
 A_{n/2,2}&\ge R_4^{n/4}\ge1,\\
 A_{n/2,k}&\ge R_n\ge1\qquad(k\ge3).
\end{align*}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $k=3$ use Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-three}.  Since $R_n\ge1$, apex-number lifting with
$s=3$ gives the same relative inequality for all $k\ge3$.
For $k=2$, the conditional spectral bound, moment monotonicity, and the reference mean give
\[
 A_{n/2,2}\ge\E(\QQ2)^n
 \ge\bigl(\E(\QQ2)^4\bigr)^{n/4}\ge R_4^{n/4}\ge1.
\]
For $k=1$, $Z_1=1+b>0$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-support} gives
\[
 \E(\QQ1)^4\ge\frac{X^2}{1+b}.
\]
Here $X\ge1+2b+c/3\ge1+b$, so $X^2/(1+b)\ge1+b\ge1$.
Apply the conditional spectral bound and moment monotonicity once more.
Complementation removes the temporary assumption $m\ge0$ without changing any of these
quantities or inequalities.
\end{proof}

\section{Passage from finite kernels to arbitrary graphons}
\label{sec:approx}

This section is an additional formalization route.  It proves that the finite-dimensional
argument already establishes the theorem on the full graphon space.  It is not a restriction
to finite-step graphons and uses no uniform bound on the number of cells.

Let $I=[0,1]$ with Lebesgue probability measure.  Products are equipped with product
measure; completion does not change any integral of the bounded functions in use.

\begin{lemma}[A pointwise bounded symmetric representative]
\label{lem:representative}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.symmetric_bounded_representative}
\uses{lem:density-algebra}
\proved Every a.e. symmetric Lebesgue-measurable $W:I^2\to\R$ with $0\le W\le1$ a.e. has
a Borel-measurable representative $\widetilde W:I^2\to[0,1]$ that is symmetric at every
point.  Replacing $W$ by this representative leaves every finite simple graph density
unchanged.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
A Lebesgue-measurable real function on $I^2$ agrees a.e. with a Borel-measurable function.
This follows, for example, by approximating the function with measurable simple functions
and replacing each set in the approximation by a Borel set differing by a null set; the
countable union of exceptional sets is null.  Choose such a representative $W_0$, clip it
to $[0,1]$, and set
\[
 \widetilde W(x,y)=\frac{\max(0,\min(1,W_0(x,y)))+
                             \max(0,\min(1,W_0(y,x)))}2.
\]
This is Borel, symmetric, and $[0,1]$-valued.  Symmetry of the original kernel a.e. and
measure preservation of $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$ show that it agrees with $W$ a.e.
Lemma~\ref{lem:density-algebra} proves invariance of all densities.  The statement is a
standard measurable-representative fact; the finite-first proof could alternatively carry
a.e. equivalence classes throughout.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Dyadic cell averages]
\label{def:dyadic}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.dyadicAverage}
\uses{def:densities}
For $j\ge0$ let $d_j=2^j$, and partition $I$ into $d_j$ dyadic intervals of length $1/d_j$.
Use half-open intervals except that the last interval contains $1$.  Denote the cells by
$I_{j,a}$, $0\le a<d_j$.  For integrable $F:I^2\to\R$, set
\[
 \overline F_j(a,b)=d_j^2\int_{I_{j,a}\times I_{j,b}}F,
 \qquad
 (P_jF)(x,y)=\overline F_j(a,b)
 \quad\bigl((x,y)\in I_{j,a}\times I_{j,b}\bigr).
\]
For the signed kernel $U$, write $U_j=P_jU$ and $W_j=(1+U_j)/2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Contraction and elementary properties of cell averages]
\label{lem:dyadic-properties}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.dyadic_average_properties}
\uses{def:dyadic}
\proved The map $P_j$ is linear and
\[
 \|P_jF\|_{L^1}\le\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad \iint P_jF=\iint F.
\]
If $U$ is symmetric and $|U|\le1$ a.e., then $U_j$ is a pointwise symmetric step kernel
with $|U_j|\le1$.  If $F$ is constant on the cells of some dyadic level $j_0$, then
$P_jF=F$ a.e. for all $j\ge j_0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Linearity holds on each cell.  If $C$ is a product cell of measure $d_j^{-2}$, its
contribution to $\|P_jF\|_1$ is $|\int_C F|\le\int_C|F|$.  Sum over the finite partition.
The integral identity is the same computation without absolute values.
The average of a function in $[-1,1]$ belongs to that interval.  Swapping the two cell
coordinates and using symmetry proves $\overline U_j(a,b)=\overline U_j(b,a)$.
A finer dyadic cell is contained in one cell at level $j_0$, so the average of a constant
on that cell is the same constant.  Endpoint choices have measure zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Density of dyadic step functions in $L^1$]
\label{lem:dyadic-density}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.dyadic_step_dense_in_L1}
\uses{def:dyadic}
\proved For every bounded measurable $F:I^2\to\R$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a
function $G$ constant on one finite dyadic partition with $\|F-G\|_1<\varepsilon$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\mathcal A$ be the algebra of finite unions of dyadic product cells, allowing a common
refinement so that every finite union is at one level.  It generates the Borel sets of
$I^2$, because dyadic endpoints are dense and open rectangles are countable unions of such
half-open cells, up to boundary sets.  The harmless endpoint sets may be added to the
algebra and have measure zero.

The class of measurable sets $E$ such that, for every $\eta>0$, some $A\in\mathcal A$
satisfies $\lambda^2(E\mathbin\triangle A)<\eta$, is a sigma-algebra.  For complements use
$E^c\triangle A^c=E\triangle A$.  For finite unions use the union bound on symmetric
differences.  For a countable union $E=\bigcup_iE_i$, finite measure and continuity from
below give a finite partial union within any prescribed error of $E$; approximate its
finitely many constituent sets and use the finite-union estimate.  This sigma-algebra
contains $\mathcal A$ and therefore every Borel set.  Every Lebesgue-measurable set differs
from a Borel set by a null set, so it has the same approximation property.

Quantize the bounded range of $F$ into finitely many intervals of length less than
$\varepsilon/2$, obtaining a measurable simple function
$F_0=\sum_{i=1}^q c_i\one_{E_i}$ with $\|F-F_0\|_1<\varepsilon/2$.
Choose $A_i\in\mathcal A$ so that
$\sum_i|c_i|\lambda^2(E_i\triangle A_i)<\varepsilon/2$; terms with $c_i=0$ impose no
condition.  Then $G=\sum_i c_i\one_{A_i}$ is constant on a common finite dyadic refinement
and has $\|F-G\|_1<\varepsilon$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Dyadic convergence]
\label{lem:dyadic-convergence}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.dyadic_average_tendsto_L1}
\uses{lem:dyadic-properties,lem:dyadic-density}
\proved For every bounded measurable $F:I^2\to\R$,
\[
 \|P_jF-F\|_1\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular $U_j\to U$ in $L^1$, and $m(U_j)=m(U)$ at every level.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a dyadic step $G$ with $\|F-G\|_1<\varepsilon/2$.
For all sufficiently large $j$, $P_jG=G$ a.e.  Contraction gives
\[
 \|P_jF-F\|_1
 \le\|P_j(F-G)\|_1+\|G-F\|_1<\varepsilon.
\]
The mean identity is already in Lemma~\ref{lem:dyadic-properties}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Density continuity with an explicit bound]
\label{lem:L1-counting}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.homDensity_L1_lipschitz}
\uses{def:densities}
\proved Let $F$ have $e\ge1$ edges.  If $|L|,|L'|\le B$ a.e., with $B\ge1$, then
\[
 |t(F,L)-t(F,L')|\le eB^{e-1}\|L-L'\|_{L^1(I^2)}.
\]
For an edgeless graph both densities are one.  Consequently, for $U,V\in[-1,1]$,
\[
 |A_{n/2,k}(U)-A_{n/2,k}(V)|
 \le n(k+1)\,2^{n(k+1)-1}\|U-V\|_1,
\]
\[
 |R_n(U)-R_n(V)|\le n2^{n-1}\|U-V\|_1.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate the edges as $e_1,\ldots,e_e$ and use
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^e a_i-\prod_{i=1}^e b_i
 =\sum_{j=1}^e(a_j-b_j)\prod_{i<j}a_i\prod_{i>j}b_i.
\]
All factors except the difference have absolute value at most $B$.  The integral of the
absolute difference on a single edge is $\|L-L'\|_1$, since its two formal endpoints are
distinct product coordinates and all unused coordinates have measure one.  Integrate the
triangle inequality and sum.  For $A,R$ use the signed-color normalization with
$|S_\sigma|\le2$ and $|S_\sigma(U)-S_\sigma(V)|=|U-V|$, then average the two colours.
The constants need not be uniform in $n,k$: each pair is fixed before taking a limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A step density equals the corresponding matrix density]
\label{lem:step-matrix}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.dyadic_homDensity_eq_matrix}
\uses{def:dyadic,def:densities}
\proved For every finite simple graph $F$ with $v$ vertices,
\[
 t(F,U_j)=d_j^{-v}\sum_{\phi:V(F)\to\Fin(d_j)}
                       \prod_{\{u,v\}\in E(F)}\overline U_j(\phi(u),\phi(v)).
\]
The same holds with $U_j$ replaced by $1\pm U_j$ or $W_j$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Partition the vertex-coordinate product space according to the cell of each coordinate.
For a fixed map $\phi$, the product is constant and the product cell has measure $d_j^{-v}$.
Summing over all maps proves the equality.  No map is excluded when two vertices belong
to the same cell.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Integral scalar moments for graphons]
\label{def:integral-scalars}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.graphonScalars}
\uses{def:densities}
For $U=2W-1$, define
\[
 f(x)=\int_IU(x,y)\,dy,\quad m=\int_If,\quad a=m^2,\quad b=\int_If(x)^2\,dx,
\]
\[
 K(x,z)=\int_IU(x,y)U(z,y)\,dy,\quad
 c=t(C_4,U),\quad r=c^{1/4},\quad p_3=t(P_3,U),\quad\tau=t(C_3,U),
\]
where $P_3$ is the path with three edges.  Put
\[
 q=\iint f(x)U(x,y)K(x,y)\,dx\,dy,
 \qquad X=1+2a+8b+c+4q.
\]
The same symbols agree with the finite definitions on every equal-cell step kernel.
In the note's operator terminology, $c=\Tr T_U^4$ and $K$ is the kernel of $T_U^2$.
The proof below only needs the integral identities.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Integral identities and continuity of the scalar moments]
\label{lem:integral-moments}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.integral_scalar_identities}
\uses{def:integral-scalars,lem:L1-counting,lem:diamond,lem:fourth-traces,lem:density-algebra}
\proved For graphons,
\[
 b=t(P_2,U)\ge0,\quad
 c=\iint K(x,z)^2\,dx\,dz\ge0,\quad
 R_4=1+2a+4b+c.
\]
The diamond identity and bound remain valid:
\[
 X=\E\Pi_1\ge1+2b+c/3,
\]
where the last expression can equivalently be read as the diamond graph density without
introducing conditional operators.  If $U_j\to U$ in $L^1$ with $|U_j|\le1$, then
$m_j,a_j,b_j,c_j,p_{3,j},\tau_j,q_j,X_j$ converge to the corresponding quantities of $U$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fubini identifies $t(P_2,U)$ with $\int f^2$.  Splitting the four-cycle between two opposite
vertices identifies it with $\int K^2$.  The fourth-cycle and diamond expansions in
Lemmas~\ref{lem:fourth-traces} and~\ref{lem:diamond} were finite product expansions, so their
integral versions apply.  The proof $|q|\le\sqrt{bc}$ uses exactly the same Cauchy--Schwarz
argument on $I^2$.

Each of $m,b,c,p_3,\tau,q$ is a density of a fixed simple signed graph: respectively an edge,
a two-edge path, a four-cycle, a three-edge path, a triangle, and a triangle with a pendant
edge.  Their continuity follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:L1-counting}; $a$ and $X$ are finite
polynomial combinations of them.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unrestricted graphon inequalities]
\label{thm:graphon-main}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.all_even_graphon_apex_bounds}
\uses{thm:finite-main,lem:representative,lem:dyadic-properties,lem:dyadic-convergence,lem:step-matrix,lem:L1-counting,lem:integral-moments}
\proved For every graphon, every even $n\ge4$, and every $k\ge1$,
\begin{align*}
 A_{n/2,1}&\ge\left(\frac{X^2}{1+b}\right)^{n/4}\ge1,\\
 A_{n/2,2}&\ge R_4^{n/4}\ge1,\\
 A_{n/2,k}&\ge R_n\ge1\qquad(k\ge3).
\end{align*}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Replace $W$ by the representative in Lemma~\ref{lem:representative}.  Fix $n,k$.
For each $j$, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-main} to the symmetric matrix
$\overline U_j\in[-1,1]^{d_j\times d_j}$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:step-matrix} identifies every density
in that theorem with its step-kernel integral.

By $L^1$ convergence and Lemma~\ref{lem:L1-counting}, the left sides tend to the corresponding
densities of $U$.  For $k\ge3$, the right side $R_n(U_j)$ tends to $R_n(U)$.
For $k=2$, use continuity of $x\mapsto x^{n/4}$ on $[0,\infty)$ and $R_4(U_j)\to R_4(U)$.
For $k=1$, $1+b_j\ge1$, so division is continuous and
$X_j^2/(1+b_j)\to X^2/(1+b)$.  These ratios are nonnegative.  Real-power continuity again
applies.  The order relation $\ge$ is closed under limits of real sequences.
Finally $R_n(U_j)\ge1$ implies $R_n(U)\ge1$, and
$X\ge1+2b+c/3\ge1+b$ proves the explicit absolute lower bound for $k=1$.
Since $n,k$ were arbitrary, all quantified inequalities follow.
\end{proof}

\section{Equality without infinite-dimensional spectral theory}
\label{sec:equality}

A limit of strict inequalities need not be strict.  This section supplies the separate
argument required for the equality statement; it does not infer strictness from the strict
finite-host results.

\begin{lemma}[A vanishing fourth signed cycle determines the kernel]
\label{lem:c-zero}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.fourth_signed_cycle_zero_iff}
\uses{lem:integral-moments,def:dyadic,lem:dyadic-convergence}
\proved For a bounded symmetric signed kernel on $I^2$,
\[
 c=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad U=0\text{ almost everywhere}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $c=0$, the identity $c=\int K^2$ gives $K=0$ a.e.  For every dyadic interval $A\subseteq I$,
Fubini gives
\[
 \int_I\left(\int_A U(x,y)\,dx\right)^2dy
 =\int_{A\times A}K(x,x')\,dx\,dx'=0.
\]
Thus $\int_AU(x,y)\,dx=0$ for a.e. $y$.  Its integral over any dyadic interval $B$ is zero,
so $\int_{A\times B}U=0$.  Every dyadic cell average of $U$ is therefore zero.  Hence
$P_jU=0$ for every $j$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:dyadic-convergence} implies $\|U\|_1=0$, which is
$U=0$ a.e.  The reverse implication follows from the density definition.
No value of $U$ or $K$ on a geometric diagonal is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite spectral interpolation for a remainder]
\label{lem:spectral-interpolation}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.finite_spectral_remainder_interpolation}
\uses{lem:moment-basics}
\proved If $x_1,\ldots,x_d\ge0$ and the integer $n>4$, then
\[
 \sum_i x_i^4
 \le\left(\sum_i x_i^2\right)^{(n-4)/(n-2)}
     \left(\sum_i x_i^n\right)^{2/(n-2)}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Put $A=\sum_i x_i^2$.  If $A=0$ all $x_i$ vanish.  Otherwise give index $i$ probability
$x_i^2/A$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:moment-basics} to $Y_i=x_i^2$, at exponent
$q=(n-2)/2>1$.  It gives
\[
 \frac{\sum_i x_i^n}{A}
 \ge\left(\frac{\sum_i x_i^4}{A}\right)^{(n-2)/2}.
\]
Raise both sides to the positive power $2/(n-2)$ and rearrange.  All divisions are by $A>0$.
Zero weights or zero $x_i$ cause no difficulty.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A fourth-trace bound near even-trace equality]
\label{lem:spectral-concentration}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.finite_fourth_trace_from_even_trace}
\uses{lem:finite-spectral,lem:spectral-interpolation}
\proved Let $B$ be a finite real symmetric matrix with $\Tr B^2\le4$.  Suppose there is a
unit vector $e$ with $\inner e{Be}\ge1$.  For an even integer $n>4$, put $t=\Tr B^n$.
Then $t\ge1$ and
\[
 1\le\Tr B^4
 \le t^{4/n}+4^{(n-4)/(n-2)}(t-1)^{2/(n-2)}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The largest eigenvalue $\lambda$ is at least the Rayleigh value, so $\lambda\ge1$.
Write the remaining eigenvalues as $\lambda_i$.  Since $n$ is even,
\[
 \sum_i|\lambda_i|^n=t-\lambda^n\le t-1,
 \qquad\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2\le4,
 \qquad\lambda^4\le t^{4/n}.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral-interpolation} to the remaining absolute eigenvalues and add
$\lambda^4$.  The lower bound follows from $\lambda\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Equality in the even-cycle bound for graphons]
\label{lem:even-cycle-equality}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.even_cycle_equality_iff_constant}
\uses{thm:graphon-main,lem:finite-even-cycle,lem:dyadic-properties,lem:dyadic-convergence,lem:L1-counting,lem:step-matrix,lem:spectral-concentration,lem:integral-moments,lem:c-zero}
\proved For every graphon and even $n\ge4$,
\[
 R_n=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W=1/2\text{ almost everywhere}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The reverse implication follows by evaluating every edge at $1/2$.  Suppose $R_n=1$ and
use the dyadic approximations.  Since $m(U_j)=m(U)$, the finite lower bound and density
continuity give
\[
 1=R_n(U)\ge1+\binom n2m(U)^2.
\]
Thus $m(U)=0$, and every finite approximation has mean zero.

If $n=4$, the identity $R_4=1+2a+4b+c$ gives $c=0$ immediately.  Suppose $n>4$.
Let $t_{\sigma,j}=\Tr T_{S_\sigma(U_j)}^n$.  The unit constant vector has Rayleigh value one,
so $t_{\sigma,j}\ge1$.  Their average is $R_n(U_j)\to1$, and consequently
\[
 0\le t_{\sigma,j}-1\le2(R_n(U_j)-1)\longrightarrow0
\]
for each colour.  Also
\[
 \Tr T_{S_\sigma(U_j)}^2
 =d_j^{-2}\sum_{a,b}S_\sigma(\overline U_j)_{ab}^2\le4.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:spectral-concentration} to these finite matrices.  Both real powers
on its right side are continuous at the indicated limits, so
$\Tr T_{S_\sigma(U_j)}^4\to1$.  Hence $R_4(U_j)\to1$.
Density continuity identifies this limit as $R_4(U)$, giving $R_4(U)=1$ and $c=0$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:c-zero} now gives $U=0$ a.e., equivalently $W=1/2$ a.e.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Equality and the final normalization]
\label{cor:main-equality}
\lean{EvenCycleApex.commonality_equality_iff_constant}
\uses{thm:graphon-main,lem:c-zero,lem:even-cycle-equality,lem:integral-moments,def:normalization,lem:counts}
\proved Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, including its equality statement, holds.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:graphon-main} gives $A_{n/2,k}\ge1$ for every stated pair $(n,k)$.
Dividing by the positive number $2^{n(k+1)-1}$ gives the claimed commonality inequality.

Suppose $U$ is not equal to zero almost everywhere, that is,
$\lambda^2(\{(x,y):U(x,y)\ne0\})>0$.  Then $c>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:c-zero}.  For $k=1$,
\[
 X\ge1+2b+c/3>1+b,
 \qquad\frac{X^2}{1+b}>1+b\ge1.
\]
The one-apex bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:graphon-main} is therefore strictly larger than one.
For $k=2$, $R_4=1+2a+4b+c>1$, so its bound is also strict.
For $k\ge3$, $A_{n/2,k}\ge R_n>1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:even-cycle-equality}.
Conversely, when $U=0$ a.e., every edge of $W$ has value $1/2$ a.e. and
$M(C_n^{+k},W)=2^{1-n(k+1)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
\proves{thm:main}
\uses{thm:graphon-main,cor:main-equality}
The unrestricted inequalities are Theorem~\ref{thm:graphon-main}, and the equality and
normalization are Corollary~\ref{cor:main-equality}.
\end{proof}

The \verb|\lean| and \verb|\uses| annotations follow the documented blueprint syntax
\cite{blueprintdoc}.  No environment is marked as already formalized.

\subsection{The finite proof object, without a graph-enumeration axiom}
The literal data use lists for transport.  Before interpreting a list as a matrix or a finite
function, the checker must prove its dimensions and entry bounds.  For example, the
normalization witnesses can be interpreted as functions on $\Fin(32768)$ only after their
length is checked.  Each permutation row must be a bijection of $\Fin(6)$; checking its six
entries lie in $\{0,\ldots,5\}$ and are pairwise distinct is sufficient.

A precise proposition for the factorization part is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathsf{FactorOK}(A,L,\delta)\ :\Longleftrightarrow\;&
 \text{$A,L$ have size $d\times d$ and $\delta$ has length $d$};\\[-2pt]
 &L_{ii}=1,\quad L_{ij}=0\ (i<j),\quad\delta_i>0;\\[-2pt]
 &\forall i,j<d,\quad
 A_{ij}=\sum_{h<d}L_{ih}\delta_hL_{jh}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
All its arithmetic is over $\Q$.  There is no need to formalize the algorithm that found
$L,\delta$ if these explicit identities are checked.  Lemma~\ref{lem:ldl-soundness} proves
that every passing factorization gives the required real positive-semidefinite matrix.
Likewise, a valid relabelling witness and the coefficient equality are sufficient; a proof
that there are exactly $156$ unlabelled six-vertex graphs is not needed in the mathematical
soundness theorem.  That count is an independent check on the supplied data.

The following distinctions must be preserved in the implementation.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The four targets are constructed from the literal edge sets in
Definition~\ref{def:certificate-targets}, not copied from the right sides of the certificates.
\item Products of graph masks use edge-set union only after disjointness is proved.
There is no relation $U_e^2=U_e$ or $U_e^2=1$.  The kernel values are arbitrary reals in
$[-1,1]$.
\item The second copy of each rooted feature uses fresh nonroot variables.  Only the roots
are identified.  Root edges occur only in the type factor.
\item Missing polynomial coefficients are zero.  Equality is checked at every coefficient
position, not just at the positions containing a nonzero coefficient on one chosen side.
\item The root factors are literal products $(1\pm U)/2$; no assertion about injective
host samples, distinct host values, or conditional induced subgraphs is needed.
\end{enumerate}

The data package includes exact $LDL^{\mathsf T}$ witnesses and explicit relabelling
witnesses in addition to the four original matrix collections.  It is legitimate to import
them as literal data.  It is not legitimate to introduce a theorem saying that they are
correct solely because an external program returned success.

\subsection{Kernel-checkable arithmetic and the trust boundary}
For a small closed rational identity, a Lean proof term produced by ordinary arithmetic
normalization is sufficient.  For the larger collection, one may define a structurally
recursive Boolean checker, prove that its success implies the finite propositions above,
and prove success by kernel reduction, splitting the work into matrix blocks and coefficient
ranges as needed.  The soundness theorem and the specific successful evaluation are both
required.

The Lean reference distinguishes kernel reduction from native evaluation.  In particular,
\code{decide +kernel} uses kernel reduction, whereas \code{native_decide} (or
\code{decide +native}) enlarges the trusted computation mechanism \cite{leanmanual}.
A certificate-focused formalization should not hide this distinction.  The conservative
route is ordinary proof terms or kernel reduction of the finite checker.  No claim about
the performance of a particular unimplemented Lean checker is made here.

After completing a development, inspect the axioms of the final declarations, for example
\begin{verbatim}
#print axioms EvenCycleApex.commonality_all_even_all_apices
#print axioms EvenCycleApex.commonality_equality_iff_constant
\end{verbatim}
The expected foundational axioms are the standard Lean logical axioms used by the chosen
libraries; there should be no unfinished-proof axiom or new axiom asserting a certificate,
a numerical computation, or the universal graph inequality.  The official validation guide
explains this inspection and the role of external rechecking tools \cite{leanvalidation}.
These are acceptance conditions for a future Lean proof, not completed checks in this
package.

\subsection{Analytic contracts to preserve}
For probability-space powers, explicitly carry nonnegativity, measurability, and boundedness.
The weighted expectations use measures with densities $\omega$ and $2-\omega$; their total
mass is one and neither density is required to be strictly positive.  Natural exponents and
real exponents must be related explicitly, especially at $n/4$ and $k/s$.

For finite spectral arguments, the Euclidean constant vector has coordinates $1/\sqrt d$.
The kernel matrix is divided by $d$.  In the conditional matrix, square roots occur once at
each end of each edge; the trace expansion uses $\sqrt{h}^2=h$.  The matrices may have
negative eigenvalues.  Evenness of $n$ is used exactly where a trace becomes a sum of
nonnegative eigenvalue powers.

For graphons, the final passage uses only $L^1$ continuity of fixed finite graph densities.
It does not require continuity of the conditional quotient or of eigenvalues of varying
infinite-dimensional operators.  The equality proof uses a quantitative finite-matrix
remainder estimate before passing to the limit, rather than a limit of strict inequalities.

For the normalized commonality statement, graph edge counts and powers of $2$ are proved
before converting to the unnormalized bound.  In the apex-moment lemma the finite measure
has mass $R_n$, not one; only its normalization by $R_n$ is a probability measure.

\subsection{Dependency bottlenecks and source correspondence}
The central dependency chains are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \text{rational factor and coefficient checks}
 \Longrightarrow \text{four universal polynomial inequalities},\\
 \text{conditional second spectral moment}
 +\text{two mean certificates}
 \Longrightarrow \text{reference fourth mean},\\
 G,H+\text{scalar amplification}+\text{majority bounds}
 \Longrightarrow \text{weighted fourth comparison},\\
 \text{two fourth-moment comparisons}
 \Longrightarrow \text{all lengths for three apices}
 \Longrightarrow \text{all larger apex numbers},\\
 \text{finite-host bounds}+L^1\text{ approximation}
 \Longrightarrow \text{all graphons},\\
 \text{finite spectral remainder bound}+c=0\Longleftrightarrow U=0
 \Longrightarrow \text{equality characterization}.
 \end{gathered}
\]

\section{Reproduction, audit, and exact data access}
\label{sec:reproduction}

\subsection{What was executed}
The unchanged source checker was rerun on all four certificates.  It checks $624$
isomorphism-class coefficient equalities and $956$ positive leading principal minors.
The source auxiliary checker verifies the two weighted algebra identities, the shifted
scalar polynomial, and exact finite-host consistency cases.

The separate audit described in Proposition~\ref{prop:checked-data} was also run.  It checks
$32768$ explicit relabelling witnesses, all $131072$ normalized coefficient positions across
the four identities, and all $13708$ entries in $76$ rational matrix factorizations with
$956$ positive rational diagonal factors.  It uses no import from the original checkers.
These finite arithmetic statements are not floating-point tests.

The provided Lean data file contains only definitions of the integer matrices.  It contains
no theorem proving positivity or correctness, and it has not been compiled in Lean.  The
JSON factor and permutation files provide optional witnesses for a future Lean checker;
the checker must validate them, not trust their filenames or hashes.

\subsection{Commands}
In the bundle root run
\begin{verbatim}
sh run_verification.sh
\end{verbatim}
This places the unchanged source programs with their input files in a temporary directory,
runs them, and then runs the independent audit.  Only Python's standard library is needed.
The source checker rejects assertion-disabling execution.  The independent checker uses
explicit exceptions for every failed assertion.

To regenerate the optional witness files and the literal Lean matrix definitions, run
\begin{verbatim}
python3 checks/independent_audit.py \
  --certificates certificates --export lean-data
\end{verbatim}
To compile the organized printable version,
\begin{verbatim}
cd blueprint/src
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error print.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error print.tex
\end{verbatim}
The top-level standalone file \code{even_apex_blueprint.tex} includes the entire mathematical
content, the four exact matrix files, and all three arithmetic programs.  Compiling it in a
fresh directory writes those embedded files; it does not execute any of the programs.
For extraction without TeX, the bundle also supplies a script that accepts only local
filenames and writes the embedded contents to a specified directory.

The PDF has been compiled and visually inspected.  The organized \code{web.tex} is a
blueprint input for a future Lean project; no HTML build or declaration-existence check is
claimed.  The declaration names and dependency annotations are proposed implementation
metadata.

\section{What is proved and what remains}
\label{sec:status}
\textbf{Proved mathematically, with exact finite certificates.}
Every even cycle with every positive independent apex number is common on arbitrary
graphons; the relative inequality holds for $k\ge3$; equality in commonality holds exactly
at $W=1/2$ a.e.  The finite-dimensional proof, its passage to arbitrary graphons, and the
equality argument have all been supplied.  Every rational matrix and every necessary
finite target is specified, and both arithmetic replays succeeded.

\textbf{Remaining formalization work.}
The proposed Lean declarations must be implemented and compiled, the finite arithmetic
must be rechecked inside the chosen Lean trust boundary, and the final theorem and its
axioms must be inspected.  No unfinished Lean proof is represented as a completed one.
The mathematical statement does not include the global relative inequality for two apices
or a theorem for every Sidorenko base graph; neither is needed for the result above.
